claims.statement: Cleopatra VII Philopator was born in early 69 BC (some sources allow late 70 BC), daughter of Ptolemy XII Auletes; her mother is not identified with certainty.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The day and month are not known.

claims.statement: She was of Macedonian Greek descent, from the dynasty founded by Ptolemy I Soter; her first language was Koine Greek, and she is the only Ptolemaic ruler known to have learned the Egyptian language.

Plutarch writes that her tongue, 'like an instrument of many strings', could turn to whatever language she pleased, and that she seldom needed an interpreter with Ethiopians, Troglodytes, Hebrews, Arabians, Syrians, Medes, or Parthians.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Plutarch wrote more than a century later; he reports this as fact.

claims.statement: She was queen of Egypt from 51 BC to 30 BC.
Her first child, a son, Ptolemy Caesar, called Caesarion, was born in 47 BC, possibly on 23 June; Plutarch says he 'was believed to be' the son of the Roman dictator.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The birth date is uncertain. Nothing is recorded about the pregnancy or the birth.

claims.statement: Mark Antony summoned her to Cilicia in 41 BC; she drew him to Alexandria, where he spent the winter of 41 to 40 BC with her, and he left Egypt by the spring of 40 BC.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The twins were conceived during this winter.

claims.statement: By the end of 40 BC she had borne twins, a son, Alexander Helios, and a daughter, Cleopatra Selene; Cassius Dio calls them 'twins at a birth', and Mark Antony later acknowledged them as his children.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The month of the birth is not recorded. Nothing is recorded about the pregnancy or the birth; chorionicity, a modern concept, cannot be known.

claims.statement: By the summer of 36 BC she had a third child with Mark Antony, a son, Ptolemy Philadelphus.

She died by suicide in Alexandria in August 30 BC, on about 10 or 12 August, at 39, after the Roman capture of the city. Ancient writers did not agree on how she died; Plutarch writes that 'the truth of the matter no one knows'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded once, without method detail. The date is a Roman (Julian) date and uncertain by a day or two.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluation of a uterus large for dates in early pregnancy (dating by the last period checked against the crown-rump length under ACOG Committee Opinion 700; multiple pregnancy, dating error, fibroids, and molar pregnancy) and high-risk prenatal care of a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy in a 29-year-old woman under ACOG Practice Bulletin 231 and Committee Opinion 831: chorionicity from the first-trimester scan, aneuploidy screening options in twins (nuchal translucency for each fetus, cell-free DNA, and diagnostic testing), nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, iron deficiency anemia and iron, low-dose aspirin because a twin pregnancy is a high-risk factor for preeclampsia (USPSTF 2021), detailed anatomy scans, growth scans every four weeks with discordance, preterm birth risk and cervical length without cerclage, progesterone, or bed rest for twins alone (ACOG Practice Bulletin 234), gestational diabetes screening, Tdap and seasonal vaccines, a viral gastroenteritis with tightenings at 22 weeks, perinatal mood screening with the EPDS (ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline 4), and a delivery plan for 38 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks. The episode ends at 33 weeks, before delivery.

hpi.narrative: Cleopatra returns at 11 weeks 0 days by her last period. This morning's ultrasound with Dr. Haddad-Thornbury of maternal-fetal medicine showed two live fetuses with a thick dividing membrane and a twin-peak sign: a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. The crown-rump lengths (45 and 46 mm) agree with her dates within three days, so her due date is unchanged. There are no fibroids and no features of a molar pregnancy. The nausea has eased on doxylamine with pyridoxine; she vomits about once a day and keeps food and fluids down (PUQE 7). She takes the prenatal vitamin and ferrous sulfate every other day. She has had no bleeding or pain. She was surprised by the news of twins and is pleased, though she is already thinking about how she will manage her work. Her first-visit results are back.

hpi.narrative: Cleopatra is a 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, at 22 weeks 0 days with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, who came in the same day after a day and a half of vomiting (five times yesterday, once this morning) and watery diarrhea about six times a day, after a meal at which two of her guests became ill in the same way. Since last night she has felt painless tightenings of the bump about twice an hour, which ease when she rests and drinks. She has had no bleeding, no leaking of fluid, no pelvic pressure, no period-like or back pain, and no fever above 37.5 C. Both babies are moving. She has kept down small sips of an oral rehydration drink since the early morning but is passing less urine. She takes aspirin 81 mg at bedtime, ferrous sulfate every other day, and a prenatal vitamin; she stopped the doxylamine with pyridoxine three weeks ago.

assessment_plan.display: Acute viral gastroenteritis with mild dehydration
assessment_plan.assessment: Probably norovirus, given the shared meal. Mild dehydration with ketonuria; sodium 135 mmol/L, potassium 3.5 mmol/L, and creatinine 0.55 mg/dL. Dehydration can bring on uterine irritability; the tightenings are infrequent and settling, the cervix is long and closed and unchanged, and there is no bleeding or leaking, so this is not preterm labor. No stool tests or antibiotics are needed
plan: Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent sips, at least 2 to 3 liters a day while the diarrhea lasts, then a normal diet
No anti-diarrheal medicine; ondansetron is not needed because the vomiting is settling
Hand washing and bleach-based cleaning; no preparing food for others until two days after the symptoms stop
Come in at once for regular or painful tightenings (four or more an hour), bleeding, leaking fluid, pelvic pressure, inability to keep fluids down, fainting, or reduced movements
Nurse telephone check tomorrow

referral.question: Second pregnancy at 9 weeks by a certain last menstrual period, with the uterus about 12 to 13 weeks in size and heavier nausea than in her first pregnancy. Please perform a first-trimester ultrasound at 11 weeks to establish the dates and the cause of the large uterus, and advise on her prenatal care
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks; sooner for bleeding, pain, or severe vomiting
referral.pertinent_history: Cleopatra is a 29-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, whose son was born seven years ago after an uncomplicated pregnancy, by her account. Her periods are regular every 28 days and she is certain of her last period, which gives 9 weeks 0 days today. On bimanual examination the uterus is smooth and about 12 to 13 weeks in size. She has nausea most of the day with vomiting two or three times a day, but keeps fluids down (PUQE 9) and has not lost weight; urine ketones negative. No bleeding or pain. Blood pressure 108/66 mmHg; height 165 cm, weight 58.0 kg. Quantitative hCG 152,000 mIU/mL, within the wide normal range for 9 weeks. Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, MCV 79 fL, ferritin 14 ng/mL; she starts ferrous sulfate every other day today, with a prenatal vitamin and doxylamine with pyridoxine at bedtime. Other first-visit tests are pending. She had the influenza vaccine today. EPDS 6. No medical history, medicines, or allergies otherwise. She wishes to consider aneuploidy screening
questions: What explains the large uterus: a dating error, a multiple pregnancy, fibroids, or a molar pregnancy?
If there is more than one fetus, what is the chorionicity, and what surveillance will she need?
Which aneuploidy screening options suit her pregnancy?
How should her iron deficiency anemia be managed?
What should be done to assess and lower the risk of preterm birth?
When and where should she plan to give birth?

consultant_note.history: Cleopatra is seen at the request of Dr. Arvanitis-Osei at 11 weeks 0 days. Her first pregnancy, seven years ago, went to term without complications, by her account, with a vaginal birth. She has regular cycles and a certain last period. Nausea has eased on doxylamine with pyridoxine. No bleeding or pain. No family history of twins that she knows of and no fertility treatment. She leads a demanding business and wants to keep working; she prefers clear plans and women clinicians
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Today's first-trimester ultrasound: two live intrauterine fetuses; a thick dividing membrane meeting a fused anterior placental mass in a twin-peak (lambda) sign; crown-rump lengths 45 mm (11 weeks 2 days) and 46 mm (11 weeks 3 days); nuchal translucency 1.6 and 1.8 mm; nasal bones present; no structural abnormality seen; no fibroids; normal ovaries; no features of a molar pregnancy. First-visit tests: hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, MCV 79 fL, ferritin 14 ng/mL; hCG 152,000 mIU/mL; blood group A RhD positive, antibody screen negative; rubella immune; hepatitis B, HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis C negative; urine culture no growth. Today's blood pressure 106/64 mmHg and weight 58.2 kg

exam.finding: Well
Uterus about 14 weeks in size; non-tender
Two fetal hearts, 162 and 158 per minute

assessment.assessment: Explained by a twin pregnancy. Her dates stand: the crown-rump lengths differ from her last period by three days or less, within the seven days that would call for redating before 14 weeks. No fibroids or molar features, and the hCG fits twins

Dichorionic diamniotic by the twin-peak sign and the thick membrane, determined before 14 weeks, when the assessment is most accurate. Dichorionic twins avoid twin-to-twin transfusion but carry higher risks of preterm birth, preeclampsia, growth restriction and discordance, gestational diabetes, anemia, and postpartum hemorrhage than a single pregnancy
Iron needs are higher with twins; oral iron should be tried first and checked in the second trimester

recommendations: Aneuploidy screening: nuchal translucency for each twin, done today, with cell-free DNA, drawn today as she chose; in twins cell-free DNA cannot say which twin is affected and fails more often. Chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis remain available
Low-dose aspirin 81 mg at bedtime from 12 weeks until delivery, because a twin pregnancy is a high-risk factor for preeclampsia; blood pressure and urine protein at every visit
Continue ferrous sulfate every other day; check the blood count and ferritin at the anatomy-scan visit and give intravenous iron in the second trimester if they do not improve

Detailed anatomy scans of both twins at 18 to 22 weeks with placental location and a transvaginal cervical length; then growth scans every four weeks with the discordance calculated; a discordance of 20 percent or more, or a twin below the 10th centile, would need closer review
Preterm birth: teach the warning signs; do not use cerclage, a pessary, progesterone, or bed rest for a twin pregnancy alone; antenatal corticosteroids if birth before 34 weeks is threatened
Gestational diabetes screen at 24 to 28 weeks; weight gain of about 17 to 25 kg; visits every two to four weeks, every two weeks from 28 weeks

Plan birth at 38 0/7 to 38 6/7 weeks in a hospital with a neonatal intensive care unit if the pregnancy stays uncomplicated; weekly fetal testing may be considered from 36 weeks; the mode of birth depends on the presentation of twin A, to be decided in the third trimester
EPDS in each trimester and after the birth
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Arvanitis-Osei the same day. Cleopatra agrees with the plan and chose cell-free DNA screening today
consultant_note.follow_up: Primary obstetric care continues with Dr. Arvanitis-Osei. Maternal-fetal medicine will perform the anatomy and growth scans and review any discordance, and will see her again before the birth
